title: World Condemns Deadly Houthi Strike on Riyadh Airport, Calls for Immediate Action
body:
The world reacted with swift condemnation on Saturday after a missile strike by Yemen’s Houthi rebels hit Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, killing at least 12 people and injuring more than 300. The attack, the third on the Saudi capital’s main gateway in as many days, has ignited a chorus of denunciations from governments and international organisations, while U.S. President Donald Trump described the incident as “terrible” and hinted that Washington is reviewing the possibility of joining Saudi‑led operations against the Houthis.

Saudi authorities said the missiles, launched from the Red Sea‑adjacent Houthi‑controlled territories, struck the airport’s western apron, where several commercial and military aircraft were parked. Among the dead were four Saudi nationals, two Filipino workers, a Sudanese laborer and a Jordanian engineer, underscoring the multinational nature of the civilian workforce that keeps the hub running. Emergency services struggled to contain fires and clear debris, and flights were suspended for several hours, disrupting travel for thousands of passengers.

The strike comes amid an intensifying proxy war that has drawn in regional and global powers. Since the Houthis seized control of large swaths of Yemen in 2014, they have repeatedly targeted Saudi infrastructure, claiming retaliation for the kingdom’s air campaign against Houthi positions. Riyadh, in turn, has responded with a series of airstrikes across Yemen, prompting accusations of civilian casualties and humanitarian violations. The latest airport attack, however, has pushed the conflict into a new arena—civilian aviation—raising concerns about the safety of international travel routes that pass over the Red Sea and the Gulf.

International reaction was near‑uniformly condemnatory. The United Nations Secretary‑General called the bombing “a reprehensible act that must not be tolerated,” while the European Union’s foreign policy chief urged “immediate restraint” from all parties. Nations with citizens among the victims, including the Philippines, Jordan and Sudan, issued statements of sorrow and demanded a thorough investigation. The United Kingdom’s Foreign Office warned that the incident could “further destabilise an already volatile region” and signalled readiness to cooperate with any multilateral response.

President Trump’s remarks added a new dimension to the diplomatic calculus. While reiterating U.S. support for Saudi Arabia, the president said the United States was “evaluating whether we should join Saudi Arabia’s attacks on the Houthis,” a statement that sparked debate among policymakers in Washington. Some members of Congress warned that deeper U.S. involvement could entangle America in a protracted conflict with uncertain objectives, whereas others argued that a decisive response was needed to deter further attacks on civilian targets. The administration has not yet announced any concrete steps, but the rhetoric suggests a possible shift in U.S. posture that could reshape the dynamics of the Yemen war.

Analysts note that the targeting of a major international airport marks a dangerous escalation. “Airports are symbols of connectivity and economic lifelines,” said Dr. Lina Al‑Saadi, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. “When they become battlefields, the repercussions ripple far beyond the immediate casualties, affecting trade, tourism and the perception of security across the region.” The incident also highlights the growing capability of the Houthis to strike deep inside Saudi territory, a development that may prompt Riyadh to reassess its defensive measures, including the deployment of additional Patriot missile batteries and the reinforcement of its air‑defence network.

As the world watches the fallout, the focus now turns to diplomatic channels that could de‑escalate the spiralling violence. The United Nations is expected to convene an emergency meeting of the Security Council later this week, with the aim of urging restraint and exploring avenues for a ceasefire. Meanwhile, humanitarian agencies warned that further attacks on infrastructure could exacerbate the already dire conditions for millions of Yemenis caught in the crossfire. The coming days will test whether the international community can translate its condemnation into concrete actions that prevent another tragic strike on civilian targets and steer the conflict toward a negotiated resolution.
